summary: Explains how to match the strengths of public keys, symmetric keys, and the overall system when public key cryptography is used to exchange symmetric keys. A system is only as strong as its weakest link, so the sizes must be chosen consistently. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Public key cryptography is often used to hand over a symmetric key. If the public key is easier to break than the symmetric key, the attacker will break the public key instead. This document gives the numbers for choosing key sizes that match.

subtitle: How to pick an RSA or Diffie-Hellman key size that matches the symmetric key it protects.

tldr.problem: When a public key is used to protect a symmetric key, an attacker will attack whichever of the two is easier to break. The RFC says public keys and symmetric keys are often chosen without matching their strengths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models the problem with a house and a lockbox, then works out how many bits of RSA modulus or Diffie-Hellman exponent are needed to match a given symmetric key strength, using the number field sieve cost formula.
tldr.outcome: The document ends with a table mapping a required attack resistance in bits to symmetric key size, RSA or Diffie-Hellman modulus size and DSA subgroup size. It is BCP 86 from April 2004 and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Diffie-Hellman exponent size
facts.value: At least twice the symmetric key size

facts.label: Modulus for an 80-bit key, one year

today: RFC 3766 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 86, published in April 2004. It has not been obsoleted and nothing in the unit metadata updates it, so it remains the reference for matching public key strength to symmetric key strength.

sections.title: Matching Three Strengths
sections.content:
Few explanations of cryptography say how the strengths of public keys and symmetric keys relate. Picture a house with a strong lock on the front door and, next to it, a small lockbox holding the key to the front door. A burglar has two options: attack the front door lock, or attack the lockbox to get the key. Clearly the burglar is better off attacking the weaker of the two locks, so the homeowner must make sure the lockbox is at least as strong as the front door.

The same holds for a protocol. An attacker who wants a message encrypted with a symmetric key, where that key was exchanged using public key cryptography, has two options: guess the symmetric key by brute force, or work out the private key used for the exchange. A smart attacker works on the easier of the two problems. Simply choosing a very long public key is usually not a good idea, because key exchanges become much more expensive in processing time as the key length grows.

The selection procedure has four steps. First, determine the attack resistance needed to satisfy the security requirements of the application, by estimating the minimum number of computer operations the attacker must perform and taking the logarithm base two of that number, called n. A 1996 report recommended 90 bits as a good all-around choice for system security, to be increased by about 2/3 bit per year, or about 96 bits in 2005. Second, choose a symmetric cipher with a key of at least n bits and at least that much cryptanalytic strength. Third, choose a key exchange algorithm with a resistance to attack of at least n bits. Fourth, choose an authentication algorithm with a resistance to attack of at least n bits, so that a similar key exchange cannot be forged between the two parties during the secrecy lifetime of the encrypted material.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick the number of bits of protection your data needs. Then make the symmetric cipher, the key exchange and the signature all at least that strong. If any one of them is weaker, that is the one the attacker will take.

sections.title: The Two Key Exchange Methods
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman method uses a group, a generator and exponents. In today's Internet standards the group operation is based on modular multiplication. The group is defined by the multiplicative group of an integer, typically a prime p = 2q + 1 where q is a prime, with arithmetic done modulo p; the generator, often simply 2, is denoted by g.

Alice and Bob first agree, in public or in private, on the values for g and p. Alice chooses a secret large random integer a, and Bob chooses a secret random large integer b. Alice sends Bob A, which is g^a mod p; Bob sends Alice B, which is g^b mod p. Alice then computes B^a mod p and Bob computes A^b mod p. These two numbers are equal, and the participants use a simple function of this number as the symmetric key k. Diffie-Hellman can also be done over other kinds of group, for instance elliptic curves defined over finite fields, which are a particularly efficient way to compute the exchange.

For RSA key exchange, assume Bob has a public key m equal to p times q, where p and q are two secret prime numbers, an encryption exponent e and a decryption exponent d. Alice sends Bob E = k^e mod m, where k is the secret symmetric key being exchanged, and Bob recovers k by computing E^d mod m. Bob's encryption exponent e can be quite small, for example 17 bits, but his decryption exponent d will have as many bits as m does.
sections.plainLanguage: In Diffie-Hellman both sides do arithmetic modulo a large prime and end up with the same secret number without sending it. In RSA key exchange the sender encrypts the symmetric key with the recipient's public key. In both cases the attack is on the mathematics, not on guessing.

sections.title: How Hard Is the Attack
sections.content:
Factoring an RSA modulus results in complete compromise of the security of the private key. Solving the discrete logarithm problem for a Diffie-Hellman system similarly destroys the security of all key exchanges using that modulus. This document assumes the difficulty of solving the discrete logarithm problem is equivalent to the difficulty of factoring numbers of the same size as the modulus; in fact it is slightly harder, because based on empirical evidence the ratio of difficulty is at least 20 and possibly as high as 64.

The number field sieve is the best method today for solving the discrete logarithm problem. The formula for estimating the number of simple arithmetic operations needed to factor an integer n is L(n) = k * e^((1.92 + o(1)) * cubrt(ln(n) * (ln(ln(n)))^2)). By solving for k from empirical reports it appears that k is approximately 0.02, which means the effective key strength of the RSA algorithm is about 5 or 6 bits less than the naive application of the formula would imply. With the o(1) term set to 0 and k set to 0.02, for numbers in the range of 100 to 200 decimal digits, the equation becomes L(n) = 0.02 * e^(1.92 * cubrt(ln(n) * (ln(ln(n)))^2)).

Diffie-Hellman has a second attack, Pollard's rho method, whose success rate is proportional to the square root of the size of the space. Because of it, the exponent in a g^a term must be twice as large as the symmetric key. To securely derive a key of K bits, an implementation must use an exponent with at least 2*K bits. The same holds for elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, where the NFS methods are of no avail but the collision method is still effective and the multiplier still needs 2*K bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Breaking these systems means hard mathematics, not guessing. The RFC estimates that effort with a formula, and adds one extra rule: for Diffie-Hellman the secret exponent has to be twice as long as the key you want from it.

sections.title: What Bigger Numbers Cost
sections.content:
The basic result is that if you double the size of the Diffie-Hellman modular exponentiation group, you quadruple the number of operations needed for the computation. The same ratios hold for an elliptic curve group, but for equivalent security one can use smaller numbers there. Assuming on average it is about 20 times more effort to do a squaring or multiplication in an elliptic curve group than in a modular exponentiation group, and that an elliptic curve group with equivalent security to a 2048-bit modulus has about 200 bits in its representation, the relative time computes to about 5, showing that an elliptic curve implementation should be five times as fast as a modular exponentiation implementation.

RSA behaves differently. An RSA public key with a modulus of j bits has factors of about j/2 bits each. Most implementations use a small encryption exponent, so an encryption may involve as few as 16 squarings and one multiplication, and the time complexity is about 28 multiplies. Decryption must use an exponent with as many bits as the modulus, but the Chinese Remainder Theorem lets the work be done twice with a modulus of half the words and an exponent of half the bits, giving an equivalent effort of j/4 multiplies.

If the size of the RSA modulus is doubled, the multiplies take four times as long, and the decryption time doubles because the exponent is larger. The overall scaling cost is a factor of 4 for encryption and a factor of 8 for decryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Bigger numbers are not free. Doubling the size of a Diffie-Hellman group quadruples the work. Elliptic curves need much smaller numbers for the same protection, so they are several times faster.

sections.title: How Many Bits Are Enough
sections.content:
To work out how strong a public key must be, first work out how much effort it takes to break the symmetric key. The RFC works through the case where the system security requirement is 112 bits, the upper bound on the strength of TripleDES, used for illustration only.

Against a special-purpose brute-force machine, the estimate gives n = 2^2077, so moduli with about 2100 bits have the same resistance against attack as a 112-bit TripleDES key. Against conventional CPU brute force, where the symmetric key stays viable for longer, the estimate gives n = 2^2439, so moduli with about 2400 bits have the same strength as a 112-bit TripleDES key. Some authors assume the algorithms underlying the number field sieve will keep improving and recommend an even larger modulus, over 4000 bits, for protecting a 112-bit symmetric key for 50 years.

For a one-year attack, a trillionaire spending today's money buys hardware able to perform 5e12 MYs of instructions, which solves to n = 2^1195, about as many operations as it would take to crack an 80-bit symmetric key by brute force. Thus a key exchange modulus of about 1200 bits protects an 80-bit symmetric key for a secrecy requirement of one year even against a nation's resources.

Extending this logic to AES is straightforward. The 128-bit AES can be thought of as at least 16 bits stronger than TripleDES but about three times as fast, so the time and cost of a brute-force attack is approximately 2^16 more than for TripleDES, and under the assumption that 128 bits of strength is the desired goal the recommended key exchange modulus size is about 700 bits longer.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does the arithmetic for you. A 112-bit TripleDES key needs a public key of roughly 2100 to 2400 bits, depending on what the attacker is assumed to have. A 128-bit AES key needs about 700 bits more than that.

sections.title: Turning a Long Key into a Short One
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman algorithm results in a key that is hundreds or thousands of bits long, but ciphers need far fewer bits. Cryptographic one-way hash functions are the building blocks for distilling a long key into a short one, and as long as they use all of the Diffie-Hellman key to derive each block of the symmetric key, they produce keys with sufficient strength.

The usual recommendation is to use a good one-way hash function applied to the base material and to use a subset of the hash function output for the key. If the desired key length is greater than the output of the hash function, the extra bits must not reveal any information about the key exchange secret, must not be correlated with each other, and must depend on all the bits of the key exchange secret. Any good cryptographic hash function satisfies these three requirements, and even a hash function with a very short output can be iterated to produce more uncorrelated bits with a little care.

For example, SHA-1 has 160 bits of output, and SHA(DHkey) produces a good symmetric key for attack resistance of 160 bits or less. To derive 192 bits of strength, the appropriate calculation hashes the DH key again for each part, so the entropy of the DH key is not lost by iterating the hash function over the same bits. If the symmetric key must have a great deal of entropy, it is probably best to use a hash function with a large output block, 192 bits or more, rather than iterating a smaller one. Newer hash algorithms with longer output, such as SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, can be used with the same level of security.
sections.plainLanguage: The key that comes out of a key exchange is far longer than any cipher needs. Hashing it down is fine, as long as every part of the shorter key is derived from the whole secret rather than from a slice of it.

sections.title: The Table of Sizes
sections.content:
The conclusion table assumes that attackers use general-purpose computers, that the hardware is purchased in the year 2000, and that mathematical knowledge relevant to the problem remains the same. It is a pure apples-to-apples comparison of how the time for a key exchange scales with the strength requirement. The subgroup size for DSA is included, if DSA is used for supporting authentication as part of the protocol; the DSA modulus must be as long as the Diffie-Hellman modulus, but the size of the q subgroup is also relevant.

The table pairs a requirement of 70 bits of attack resistance with a 70-bit symmetric key, a 947-bit RSA or Diffie-Hellman modulus and a 129-bit DSA subgroup. 80 bits maps to 80, 1228 and 148. 90 bits maps to 90, 1553 and 167. 100 bits maps to 100, 1926 and 186. 150 bits maps to 150, 4575 and 284. 200 bits maps to 200, 8719 and 383. 250 bits maps to 250, 14596 and 482.

The RFC also carries a correction for a special-purpose sieving machine. If the TWIRL machine becomes a reality, and if there are advances in parallelism for row reduction in factoring, then conservative estimates would subtract about 11 bits from the system security column of the table. Thus, in order to get 89 bits of security, one would need an RSA modulus of about 1900 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The table at the end is the practical answer: pick the row that matches the protection you need, and use the symmetric key size, public key size and signature subgroup size given there.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The equations and values given in this document are meant to be as accurate as possible, based on the state of the art in general-purpose computers at the time the document was written. No predictions can be completely accurate, and the formulas are not meant to be definitive statements of fact about cryptographic strengths. Some of the empirical results used in calibrating the formulas are probably not completely accurate, and that inaccuracy affects the estimates. The authors' hope is that the numbers presented vary from real-world experience as little as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is careful about its own limits. These numbers are estimates from the year it was written, and it says so plainly.

items.title: 1. Set the target
items.text: Decide how many bits of attack resistance the application needs, and call that n.

items.title: 2. Choose the cipher
items.text: Pick a symmetric cipher whose key is at least n bits and has at least that much cryptanalytic strength.

items.title: 3. Choose the exchange
items.text: Pick a key exchange algorithm with at least n bits of resistance to attack.

items.title: 4. Choose the authentication
items.text: Pick an authentication algorithm with at least n bits of resistance to attack.
